britain-ashmolean.title: Ashmolean Museum: British Iron Age collections
britain-ashmolean.evidence: Archaeological chronology; 278 BCE belongs to the British Middle Iron Age, not the late coin-issuing dynasties.

maiden-castle-history.title: English Heritage: history of Maiden Castle
maiden-castle-history.evidence: Site development is phased; the largest surviving defences and later burials are not all contemporary.

snettisham-research.title: British Museum: The Snettisham Hoards
snettisham-research.evidence: Research dates the documented hoards mainly after the opening, between 150 BCE and 100 CE.

welsh-hillforts.title: National Museum Wales: Welsh Hillforts
welsh-hillforts.evidence: Archaeological interpretation; the category includes communities and defended farms of different scales and dates.

cadw-prehistory.title: Cadw: Prehistoric Wales
cadw-prehistory.evidence: Official archaeological overview; later tribal names do not precisely define earlier communities.

llanmelin-site.title: Cadw: Llanmelin Wood Hillfort
llanmelin-site.evidence: A regional hillfort example, not proof of a documented Silurian royal capital in 278 BCE.

stanwick-history.title: English Heritage: Stanwick Iron Age Fortifications
stanwick-history.evidence: The documented centre and Cartimanduan context are much later than 278 BCE.

scottish-brochs.title: Historic Environment Scotland: Mousa Broch
scottish-brochs.evidence: Regional architectural tradition; one site's date and building type cannot describe every early northern community.

irish-bog-bodies.title: National Museum of Ireland: Kingship and Sacrifice guide
irish-bog-bodies.evidence: Iron Age remains around 400–200 BCE; interpretation as kingship ritual is a hypothesis, not identification of named rulers.

irish-sea-research.title: University of Liverpool: Iron Age Irish Sea Zone
irish-sea-research.evidence: Regional archaeological research treats Wales, Ireland and the Isle of Man as connected but distinct settings.

dumnonii.text: The Dumnonian faction represents communities of southwestern Britain, not a documented kingdom whose later rulers can be carried backward into 278 BCE. The region's Iron Age history includes farming settlements, defended places and connections along the Atlantic and Channel coasts. Its position gives it a distinctive maritime setting even though the named Dumnonii become clearer in sources written centuries after the opening.
dumnonii.homeland: Southwestern Britain, broadly the later Devon–Cornwall association
dumnonii.politicalForm: Middle Iron Age regional communities under a later recorded name

sections.title: An earlier southwestern population
sections.text: Local settlement history continues from the Bronze Age into the Iron Age rather than beginning with Ptolemy's list of peoples. The later Dumnonian name provides orientation, but not a founding date or certain early royal succession. Medieval Dumnonia belongs to another political world. Neither its rulers nor its later boundaries establish the institutions of the third-century communities represented here.

sections.title: Peninsula and coastal routes
sections.text: The southwestern peninsula combines inland farming districts with access to Channel and Atlantic movement. Defended sites differ in size and chronology; not every later Cornish enclosure already exists in the opening. Metal resources contribute to the wider history of exchange, but should not become an assumed state monopoly over all British tin or proof that Greek merchants rule local settlements.

sections.title: Community life in 278 BCE
sections.text: The most secure starting units are households, local settlements and relationships between communities. Roundhouse traditions and agricultural organization reveal a social landscape more substantial than a loose band of warriors. Exact leadership titles and the reach of shared authority are unknown. A local elite can exist without a documented peninsula-wide crown, and the later ethnonym need not correspond to one fixed early state.

sections.title: The Channel and Atlantic neighbourhood
sections.text: Connections toward other British regions, Ireland and the continental coast are possible through established maritime routes. They do not prove permanent alliance or a single Celtic government spanning the sea. Rome is not an occupying power in Britain in 278, and its later provincial geography does not define the region. External relationships are primarily among indigenous communities and those participating in exchange.

sections.title: A regional start before named kingdoms
sections.text: The opening preserves a credible southwestern population and a recognizable later label. Its history is rooted in the inhabited Middle Iron Age landscape rather than an invented migration of foreign rulers. Precise tribal boundaries and named dynasties remain less secure than the region's settlement traditions and maritime position.

durotriges.text: The Durotrigan setting lies in southern Britain, especially the Dorset-associated landscape of substantial hillforts, farms and routes toward the Channel. Around 278 BCE the region is already inhabited by organized communities, but the later named people, coinages and encounter with Roman conquest belong to a different stage of its history. The opening must distinguish those phases rather than collapse them into one timeless tribal kingdom.
durotriges.homeland: Southern Britain, principally the later Dorset-associated setting
durotriges.politicalForm: Middle Iron Age settlement communities; later Durotrigan unity is not assumed

sections.title: The development of a hillfort landscape
sections.text: Sites such as Maiden Castle demonstrate long and changing occupation, with earlier activity preceding the major Iron Age settlement. Expansion of defences and internal arrangements occurred in stages. This history shows organized local communities before the Roman conquest narrative, but does not prove that every large hillfort was the capital of a separate kingdom or already shared one Durotrigan government.

sections.title: Chalk country and the Channel
sections.text: Farming districts, stored agricultural produce and connections between settlements are fundamental to the regional landscape. The Channel supplies another direction of movement rather than a barrier to all contact. Hillforts can serve several social roles as well as defence. Their most imposing surviving appearance should not automatically be assigned to 278 without regard to the site's individual chronology.

sections.title: Internal conditions in 278 BCE
sections.text: Households and communities organize cultivation, livestock and local authority. Defensive construction suggests collective resources, but does not identify a known starting king. Later coin production and social relationships cannot simply be moved backward. Archaeology gives evidence of organized everyday life while leaving the exact scale of political coordination across the region less securely documented.

sections.title: Southern British connections
sections.text: Neighbouring regions and cross-Channel exchange create opportunities for contact without requiring a single southern confederation. The Roman army's later arrival is not an existing threat from a nearby province in 278. Famous interpretations of conquest violence at Maiden Castle concern much later evidence and debate. They should not define the present condition of every community in the starting region.

sections.title: Before the coinage and conquest period
sections.text: The faction's identity provides a later historical name for an earlier inhabited region. Its starting strength comes from established local societies, not a fictional treasury of later coins or a pre-assigned Roman war. The exact third-century political relationships among hillforts and surrounding communities remain qualified.

catuvellauni.text: The Catuvellaunian faction represents an earlier southeastern British setting associated with the later powerful people of that name. In 278 BCE the well-known royal households and coinages of the late Iron Age are still far in the future. The historical foundation is instead a landscape of farming communities, enclosures and regional contacts whose precise collective identity is not recorded by contemporary written sources.
catuvellauni.homeland: Southeastern British interior, broadly the later Hertfordshire–Chiltern association
catuvellauni.politicalForm: Middle Iron Age communities; the later dynastic state is not projected backward

sections.title: Before the later southeastern dynasties
sections.text: The later political community is known through Roman accounts, archaeology and coinage of a much later period. The age of Cassivellaunus and the subsequent dynasties cannot serve as a complete early history for 278. Earlier local occupation is well established, while the timing and process through which broad political identities formed remain open questions rather than a recorded founding charter.

sections.title: An inland southeastern landscape
sections.text: The Chiltern-facing and neighbouring districts connect agricultural communities with routes toward the Thames and other regions. Hillforts and enclosed sites belong to different phases, and some were abandoned before the opening while other forms of settlement continued. The developed late Iron Age centres associated with Verlamion or Camulodunum should not appear as fully formed starting capitals.

sections.title: Internal conditions in 278 BCE
sections.text: Household organization, access to land and local networks supply a more grounded picture than an invented royal court. Differences in status are compatible with the archaeological evidence, but the exact number and authority of leaders are unknown. It would be misleading to transfer named coin-issuing rulers, their family disputes or later territorial ambitions into this earlier Middle Iron Age community grouping.

sections.title: Regional contacts before Roman intervention
sections.text: The Thames-connected world and neighbouring southeastern communities create channels for exchange and competition. Cross-Channel contact does not establish the later political relationships surrounding Caesar's expeditions. There is no Roman client kingdom here in 278. Nor does a recognizable later faction name prove that the region already commands all territories acquired by its much later rulers.

sections.title: A recognizable label for an earlier society
sections.text: The opening uses the existing regional identity while preserving the chronological distance from its best-known rulers. Local communities remain present without a fabricated dynasty or an already consolidated southeastern kingdom. Later expansion is historical perspective, not a starting entitlement over neighbouring peoples.

iceni.text: The Icenian setting lies in eastern Britain, in the region later associated with East Anglia. Its most famous rulers, revolt and spectacular gold deposits belong long after 278 BCE. The opening instead represents earlier communities of farms, local connections and varied eastern landscapes. The later ethnonym helps identify the region without turning a Roman-period people into an unchanged state existing for centuries beforehand.
iceni.homeland: Eastern Britain, broadly the later East Anglian association
iceni.politicalForm: Middle Iron Age regional communities before the documented late dynastic period

sections.title: A regional past before Boudica
sections.text: The inhabitants of eastern Britain have an Iron Age history independent of the famous first-century CE revolt. Written accounts and later coinage identify the Iceni more clearly than the earlier record does. Boudica and her family cannot provide a starting genealogy for 278. The development of the later political community should therefore be understood as a process rather than an unchanged ancient kingdom.

sections.title: Eastern farms and changing environments
sections.text: Agricultural settlement, waterways and access toward the North Sea form the local setting. Wetland and dryland districts offer different resources and connections. Modern county boundaries should not be treated as ancient frontiers. The material evidence of houses and local production matters alongside the elite objects that tend to dominate popular images of the eastern British Iron Age.

sections.title: Internal conditions in 278 BCE
sections.text: The exact scale of regional leadership is unknown, while local households and communities are archaeologically meaningful. The Snettisham hoards reveal later concentrated wealth and ritual deposition, but the documented deposits begin after this opening. They should not become an automatic starting treasury or evidence that a known royal dynasty already controlled the region. Earlier society requires its own chronology.

sections.title: Contacts across eastern Britain
sections.text: Neighbouring British communities and maritime connections offer avenues for exchange and rivalry. Rome is not yet establishing a client relationship in eastern Britain. The alliances and grievances recorded around the conquest period are later circumstances, not permanent traits of the population. Cultural links across the sea likewise do not amount to sovereignty by a continental Gallic faction.

sections.title: The eastern region before later monarchy
sections.text: The starting identity preserves an indigenous East Anglian setting without borrowing named later rulers. The historical article can acknowledge the later evidence while keeping its events separate from current affairs. In spring 278 the most secure foundations are local settlement, regional connections and a population whose precise wider political organization remains uncertain.

dobunni.text: The Dobunnian setting connects the Severn region and adjoining western British interior. It is best known through later tribal geography, coinage and Roman-period developments. In 278 BCE it belongs to an earlier world of farms, defended places and local routes rather than a fully recovered kingdom with the rulers and political divisions of the late Iron Age already established.
dobunni.homeland: The western British interior around the Severn and Cotswold-facing setting
dobunni.politicalForm: Regional Middle Iron Age communities; later political structures remain later evidence

sections.title: Before the later named community
sections.text: The archaeological landscape predates the Dobunni's fuller appearance in written history. The later name helps connect the faction with a recognizable region, but cannot date the formation of one shared government. A modern map of Roman tribal districts is therefore not a direct picture of 278. Earlier communities can have durable local identities while larger political groupings change around them.

sections.title: Severn connections and local settlement
sections.text: Valley routes, upland edges and agricultural districts connect different communities. Defended places are part of the regional story, but neither every hilltop nor every settlement phase is contemporary. The major later centre of Bagendon belongs to a different stage of political and economic development. It cannot simply furnish the opening with the urban organization and elite network visible in later centuries.

sections.title: Internal conditions in 278 BCE
sections.text: Local authority concerns land, settlement cooperation and relationships between households and leading groups. Exact spring rulers are not documented. Names reconstructed from later coinage should not be installed as ancestors with invented biographies. Nor should possible divisions in the later Dobunnian political sphere be treated as proof that the identical arrangement already existed in the Middle Iron Age.

sections.title: Between western and central Britain
sections.text: The Severn provides connections as well as local distinctions, linking this setting with Welsh-facing and southern British regions. Cross-regional exchange does not require a single island-wide Celtic state. Rome's later conquest and provincial centres do not yet organize the political landscape. The opening's external history concerns regional neighbours and movement rather than an established policy toward Roman occupation.

sections.title: An earlier Severn-region identity
sections.text: The faction begins with a plausible indigenous regional background while the precise reach of common authority remains unresolved. Its later name supplies recognition, not a fabricated crown. Roman civic foundations and late Iron Age coinage belong to subsequent chapters of the region's history.

silures.text: The Silurian faction represents communities in the southeastern Welsh setting, known much more clearly from Roman accounts of the first century CE. Their inhabitants in 278 BCE belong to a considerably earlier Iron Age society. Hillforts, defended farms and ordinary agricultural life provide a stronger starting foundation than Roman stereotypes about appearance, ancestry or an unchanging national character.
silures.homeland: Southeastern Wales and its adjoining local districts
silures.politicalForm: Iron Age local communities under a later recorded regional name

sections.title: Local history before the Roman narratives
sections.text: The Welsh Iron Age developed through centuries of settlement and cultural change. Later tribal labels offer one way of naming the landscape, but do not recover every earlier political boundary. Roman speculation about the Silures' distant ancestry is not proof of foreign colonization. The population should be understood through indigenous regional development and contact, rather than a supposed unchanging racial origin story.

sections.title: Defended places and farming communities
sections.text: The region includes substantial defended sites such as Llanmelin and many smaller settlements. Archaeological monuments can represent communities or defended farms rather than one uniform hierarchy of royal castles. Their construction and occupation phases need individual attention. Ordinary houses, fields and resource use are as important to understanding life in the region as the earthworks most visible today.

sections.title: Internal conditions in 278 BCE
sections.text: Local leaders and cooperation among communities are plausible, but no secure spring king or complete constitution is known. The ability to maintain defences demonstrates organized activity without proving a unified regional state. Later military coordination under the pressure of Roman invasion belongs to another set of circumstances. It should not replace the quieter but substantial history of everyday settlement and local authority.

sections.title: The Severn-facing regional world
sections.text: Contacts toward the Severn, neighbouring Welsh communities and wider maritime routes create several directions of connection. The people do not yet face the Roman provincial frontier familiar from later military history. Caratacus' career and campaigns belong centuries after this opening. Likewise, cultural relationships with other British groups do not establish an island-wide confederation or a permanent common foreign policy.

sections.title: An indigenous southeastern Welsh setting
sections.text: The opening preserves a local population with archaeological depth while qualifying the later tribal name. It does not fill the region with unrelated foreign rulers or replay Rome's Welsh campaigns. The exact scale of third-century political unity remains open, alongside clear evidence for organized and connected Iron Age communities.

ordovices.text: The Ordovician faction represents a northern and central Welsh regional setting whose later name is preserved in Roman geography and military history. Spring 278 BCE is much earlier than those campaigns. The landscape is already occupied by communities with local agricultural, defensive and social traditions, but it cannot be reconstructed as a fully documented tribal kingdom with an exact royal succession.
ordovices.homeland: Northern and central Welsh districts associated with later Ordovician geography
ordovices.politicalForm: Local Iron Age communities with uncertain wider political unity

sections.title: The earlier regional landscape
sections.text: Welsh settlement traditions extend across the Bronze and Iron Ages, with changes in defended sites and agricultural use. The later Ordovician identity does not provide a founding date for all those communities. Material similarities can indicate contact without proving one named state. Archaeological phases are therefore essential to avoiding the projection of Roman-period tribal geography onto an earlier political world.

sections.title: Uplands, routes and varied settlements
sections.text: The region contains uplands but also valleys, coastal access and farmland. Its inhabitants should not be reduced to isolated mountain warriors. Defended sites range in scale, and some famous monumental remains belong partly or mainly to later phases. The opening requires a landscape of local communities, not a selection of every surviving hillfort treated as a simultaneous royal capital.

sections.title: Community organization in 278 BCE
sections.text: Collective construction, farming and local resource use imply organized societies even where their leaders' names are absent. The precise relationship among communities remains difficult to recover. A later account of resistance does not establish a permanent national monarchy in this earlier spring. Political cooperation can grow or change over time without the population itself having to appear suddenly in the written record.

sections.title: The Irish Sea and neighbouring Britain
sections.text: Routes across the region and maritime connections create contact with other British communities and the Irish Sea world. These relationships do not prove that Anglesey or every neighbouring district answers to one Ordovician ruler. Later accounts of Mona and Roman military operations have their own chronology. There is no reason to begin with an already existing Roman invasion or a fixed religious war.

sections.title: A regional identity before conquest
sections.text: The opening retains indigenous Welsh communities and a recognizable later label while keeping the exact third-century borders uncertain. Their history is not dependent on future Roman resistance. Local settlement, social cooperation and wider connections provide the historical substance, with political unity treated as an approximation rather than a documented certainty.

brigantes.text: The Brigantian faction occupies a broad northern British setting, but the large political community described around the Roman conquest belongs to a later period. In 278 BCE the region contains earlier local societies whose exact shared organization is not recorded. Its historical background must therefore distinguish the landscape's long occupation from the much later careers of Cartimandua and Venutius.
brigantes.homeland: Northern British districts associated with later Brigantian geography
brigantes.politicalForm: Regional Middle Iron Age communities; later kingdom-scale unity is qualified

sections.title: Before the first-century kingdom
sections.text: The Brigantes appear prominently in Roman-period narratives and later geographical lists. Those sources describe a developed political situation, not the beginning of northern British settlement. The region's earlier agricultural and defensive landscapes have histories of their own. Political consolidation, the use of a collective name and the rise of named royal households need not all happen at the same time.

sections.title: A broad northern landscape
sections.text: Valleys, uplands and routes across northern Britain connect communities with different local resources. A large later tribal district should not be mistaken for a single homogeneous environment. Stanwick is especially important to later Brigantian power, but its documented growth and Roman-connected wealth are not a ready-made capital for 278. Earlier regional communities cannot simply inherit its final monumental form.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: Local leading groups and community organization are plausible, while an exact nationwide government remains uncertain. Evidence for later royal diplomacy does not demonstrate an unchanged dynasty reaching back to the opening. Cartimandua's alliances, personal relationships and internal conflict belong centuries later. The more responsible starting description preserves a socially organized population without inventing her distant predecessors.

sections.title: Northern Britain before the Roman frontier
sections.text: Neighbouring British regions, northern routes and maritime contacts create the relevant external setting. Roman client relations and military frontiers have not yet reached this landscape. Shared cultural practices do not require all northern communities to act as one permanent alliance. The later extent of Brigantian influence is evidence for that later political world, rather than proof of every starting possession.

sections.title: The earlier northern communities
sections.text: Spring 278 uses a broad but qualified regional identity. The population is locally rooted rather than a foreign kingdom inserted to fill northern Britain. Later monarchy, Roman patronage and the conflicts recorded by classical authors remain separate historical developments, with precise earlier political unity left unresolved.

caledonian-polities.text: The northern Scottish communities represented here belong to a varied Iron Age landscape long before Roman armies describe the Caledonians. The label is a practical regional association, not a documented united kingdom in 278 BCE. Settlement traditions, farming, local defensive works and connections across sea and land provide a real history without importing later Pictish states or medieval dynasties.
caledonian-polities.homeland: Northern Britain, especially the broad later Caledonian association
caledonian-polities.politicalForm: Several northern Iron Age communities rather than an assumed unified state

sections.title: Northern communities before Roman naming
sections.text: The inhabitants have regional histories extending through earlier prehistoric periods. Roman accounts and Ptolemy's geographical names illuminate later identities but cannot supply a precise third-century roster. Caledonian and Pictish labels belong to changing historical contexts. Neither should be treated as proof that a single continuous kingdom with one royal house already rules all northern Scotland at the opening.

sections.title: A varied northern settlement world
sections.text: Mainland and island settings contain different resources, building traditions and routes. Roundhouses and defended sites are important, but the famous broch tradition has varied and debated chronologies. Mousa's surviving tower is not a template for every settlement or proof that all such structures are already present in 278. Farms and less monumental communities remain essential to the social landscape.

sections.title: Local authority in 278 BCE
sections.text: Communities can organize substantial labour and maintain differentiated social relationships without forming one northern state. The precise leadership of each district is unknown. Monumental houses may express several kinds of local authority, and their interpretation cannot simply provide a complete constitution. Regional cooperation and competition are both plausible within a landscape whose political detail exceeds the surviving written evidence.

sections.title: Connections without an imperial frontier
sections.text: Routes link neighbouring districts, the northern seas and the wider British and Irish Sea worlds. Water can connect communities as well as separate them. Rome's northern campaigns and later frontier constructions belong centuries after the opening. There is no pre-existing Hadrianic border defining allegiance, and cultural contact does not establish sovereignty by a southern British or continental faction.

sections.title: A plural northern beginning
sections.text: The faction represents indigenous regional communities with uncertainty preserved over political unity. Later collective names assist recognition without dictating a monarchy, dynasty or permanent alliance. The starting picture is a socially organized northern world whose future relationships need not follow the later Roman narrative.

hibernian-polities.text: Ireland in 278 BCE contains indigenous Iron Age communities with local histories and connections to the wider Atlantic and Irish Sea worlds. It is not a securely documented island-wide kingdom, and its inhabitants should not be classified automatically as Brittonic. The absence of contemporary political narratives leaves real limits, but archaeology offers a richer picture than an empty island or a grid of medieval kingdoms moved backward in time.
hibernian-polities.homeland: Ireland and its indigenous regional communities
hibernian-polities.politicalForm: Several Iron Age communities; exact political geography and leadership are uncertain

sections.title: From the Bronze Age into the Iron Age
sections.text: Irish society developed through long local sequences rather than a single securely recorded Celtic invasion. Ironworking, changing styles and connections with La Tène-associated traditions form part of that development. Imported or shared artistic forms do not prove wholesale population replacement. Later Irish language and political traditions require chronological care: they cannot recover every identity, institution or boundary of the third century BCE.

sections.title: Regions, routes and ritual landscapes
sections.text: Local landscapes include agricultural districts, wetlands, routes and places with long-standing ritual significance. Archaeological sequences at famous later royal sites are complex. Their monumental or legendary importance does not establish that the named medieval provincial kingdoms already exist in 278. The island's political geography should remain regional and uncertain rather than being determined by later literature alone.

sections.title: Authority and the limits of interpretation
sections.text: Objects, settlements and exceptional human remains illuminate differences in status and ritual practice. The bog bodies associated with Oldcroghan and Clonycavan fall broadly around the centuries surrounding the opening. Their interpretation in terms of sovereignty and sacrifice is significant but debated; it does not identify named kings or prove one island-wide succession system. Local authority can be acknowledged without turning an archaeological hypothesis into a universal constitution.

sections.title: The Irish Sea and Atlantic connections
sections.text: Contacts with Britain and wider European traditions make isolation an inadequate description. Those connections are not evidence that Ireland is governed by a British, Gallic or Mediterranean state. Nor does shared Celtic-associated art require a single political or linguistic identity across the islands. Rome is absent as an occupying power, and no later recorded tribal territory should be treated as a surveyed spring 278 frontier.

sections.title: An indigenous Irish regional grouping
sections.text: The opening preserves local communities without naming speculative rulers or importing unrelated states. Its broad faction represents a region whose people have substantial historical depth but incompletely known political organization. Cultural identity remains distinct from political control, and later provincial kingdoms or medieval dynasties are not assumed to exist in their recorded forms at the start.
